title: The Membranes Pushing Seawater at 82 Bar
coreQuestion: Why does turning seawater into drinking water take so much pressure and power?
openingLine: Without pump power, desalination membranes stop making water.
secondBeat: Reverse osmosis forces it through salt-blocking membranes.
dependency: Coastal cities in dry regions depend on reverse-osmosis desalination for drinking water
mechanism: Pumps force seawater through membranes that let water pass and hold salt back
bottleneck: Overcoming seawater's natural osmotic pressure takes high pressure and energy
failureConsequence: Without pump power the membranes stop producing fresh water
expectedConsequence: water supply drops as soon as the pumps stop

narration.text: Without pump power, desalination membranes stop making water.
Seawater must be pushed through at up to 82 bar.
Seawater pushes back with about 27 bar of osmotic pressure.
So the plant's biggest energy users are its high-pressure pumps.
The salty reject stream keeps its pressure, and recovery devices reuse it.
Over time, particles and organisms foul the membrane surface.
Even state-of-the-art plants still need around 2.3 kilowatt-hours per cubic metre.
